title: Èjì Ogbè
theme: light, new beginnings, divine potential
proverb_yo: Imọ́lẹ̀ kìí ṣe n̄ǹkan tí a fún ọ — imọ́lẹ̀ ni ọ jẹ́.
proverb_en: Light is not something given to you — light is what you are.
excerpt: The senior Odu — pure light, new beginnings and the seed of all destiny.
content:
## Èjì Ogbè

> *"Imọ́lẹ̀ kìí ṣe n̄ǹkan tí a fún ọ — imọ́lẹ̀ ni ọ jẹ́."*
> *"Light is not something given to you — light is what you are."*

---

### Meaning

The senior Odu — pure light, new beginnings and the seed of all destiny.

### Associated Òrìṣà

Ọ̀rúnmìlà / Olódùmarè

### Life Lesson

You were not born by accident. Every person carries an ori (destiny) chosen before birth. Ogbè teaches that your task is to remember and fulfil your purpose, and to lead with clarity, honesty and generosity of spirit.

### Overview

Èjì Ogbè is the figure made of four open marks on both sides, the most complete expression of openness in the system. Because it is placed first, it is often described as the doorway to the other fifteen principal figures. It speaks of beginnings, of clarity, and of the moment before a path is chosen.

### Core Themes

- Clarity of purpose and honest self-presentation
- Leadership that serves rather than dominates
- The idea that every person arrives with a destiny (ori) to recognise and carry out
- Fresh starts, initiation and the opening of a season

### Everyday Guidance

When this figure is cast, tradition reads it as encouragement to act openly. Plan in the light, speak plainly, and avoid shortcuts that need to be hidden later. It also reminds a person that a good start still needs steady follow-through.

### Reflection

What would I do differently if I had nothing to hide?

title: Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Méjì
theme: endings, the ancestors, the unseen world, mortality
proverb_yo: Òkú tó sun, kì í jí mọ́; ẹ̀mí tó lọ, kì í padà bí ara.
proverb_en: The dead that sleeps does not wake again; the spirit that departs does not return in the same body.
excerpt: The Odu of endings, the ancestors, and the wisdom hidden in darkness.
content:
## Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Méjì

> *"Òkú tó sun, kì í jí mọ́; ẹ̀mí tó lọ, kì í padà bí ara."*
> *"The dead that sleeps does not wake again; the spirit that departs does not return in the same body."*

---

### Meaning

The Odu of endings, the ancestors, and the wisdom hidden in darkness.

### Associated Òrìṣà

Ikú (Death) / Ọ̀sun

### Life Lesson

Ọ̀yẹ̀kú teaches respect for the ancestors, acceptance of mortality, and the understanding that every ending clears space for renewal. It warns against arrogance in the face of life's fragility.

### Overview

Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Méjì is made of four closed marks on both sides, the mirror of Èjì Ogbè. If Ogbè is light, Ọ̀yẹ̀kú is the darkness that holds, rests and receives. In Yorùbá thought this is not only loss: night, sleep and the ancestors are part of the cycle that makes new life possible.

### Core Themes

- Respect for ancestors and elders
- Honest acceptance that life is finite
- Endings as preparation for renewal
- Rest, stillness and the value of what is not seen

### Everyday Guidance

Read in daily life, this figure asks a person to honour those who came before, settle unfinished obligations, and stop treating limits as enemies. It cautions against pride about health, wealth or status, since all of them are borrowed for a time.

### Reflection

What do I need to close properly so that something new can begin?

title: Ìwòrì Méjì
theme: self-knowledge, hidden truth, inner vision
proverb_yo: Bí a kò bá mọ ara ẹni, a kì í mọ ẹlòmíràn.
proverb_en: If one does not know oneself, one cannot truly know another.
excerpt: The Odu of self-knowledge — seeing what is hidden, including within oneself.
content:
## Ìwòrì Méjì

> *"Bí a kò bá mọ ara ẹni, a kì í mọ ẹlòmíràn."*
> *"If one does not know oneself, one cannot truly know another."*

---

### Meaning

The Odu of self-knowledge — seeing what is hidden, including within oneself.

### Associated Òrìṣà

Ọ̀sanyìn / Ọ̀rúnmìlà

### Life Lesson

Ìwòrì calls for introspection and honesty about one's own motives before judging others. It reveals secrets — both dangerous and beneficial — and teaches that true wisdom begins with self-awareness.

### Overview

Ìwòrì Méjì has a pattern of an open centre framed by closed marks, and its name is tied to the idea of looking inward and seeing. It is associated with insight, with discovering what lies beneath appearances, and with the discipline of examining one's own motives first.

### Core Themes

- Self-knowledge before judging others
- Hidden matters coming to light
- Careful observation and discernment
- Honesty in what one says about oneself

### Everyday Guidance

Tradition uses this figure to counsel reflection. Before blaming, ask what part is yours. Before trusting a story, look for what is missing from it. Insight gained this way can protect a person from deception, including self-deception.

### Reflection

What am I refusing to look at in myself?

### In the Wider System

title: Òdí Méjì
theme: the womb, mystery, transformation, hidden depth
proverb_yo: Ohun tó wà nínú, kì í fi ara rẹ̀ hàn ní ọ̀nà kan ṣoṣo.
proverb_en: What is within does not reveal itself in only one way.
excerpt: The mystery of the womb — transformation, secrets, and the depths of creation.
content:
## Òdí Méjì

> *"Ohun tó wà nínú, kì í fi ara rẹ̀ hàn ní ọ̀nà kan ṣoṣo."*
> *"What is within does not reveal itself in only one way."*

---

### Meaning

The mystery of the womb — transformation, secrets, and the depths of creation.

### Associated Òrìṣà

Ọya / Yemọja

### Life Lesson

Òdí teaches patience with processes that are not yet visible — pregnancy, growth, and transformation take time in darkness before they emerge into light. It also warns against forcing what must unfold naturally.

### Overview

Òdí Méjì is read through images of enclosure: the womb, the sealed pot, the closed door. These images are not negative. Many things must be held in a protected space before they can emerge, and this figure is a reminder that growth often happens out of sight.

### Core Themes

- Patience with slow, hidden processes
- Pregnancy, motherhood and nurture
- Protection and privacy
- Transformation that cannot be rushed

### Everyday Guidance

In practice, this figure advises a person not to uncover a plan, a project or a relationship too early. Give it time and shelter. It also warns against forcing outcomes, because pressure applied at the wrong stage can damage what is forming.

### Reflection

What in my life needs more time and shelter before it is shown?

### In the Wider System

title: Ìrosùn Méjì
theme: blood, sacrifice, warning, consequence
proverb_yo: Ẹ̀jẹ̀ tí a tú sílẹ̀ kì í padà sí inú ara.
proverb_en: Blood that is spilled does not return to the body.
excerpt: The Odu of blood and consequence — sacrifice, warning, and the price of action.
content:
## Ìrosùn Méjì

> *"Ẹ̀jẹ̀ tí a tú sílẹ̀ kì í padà sí inú ara."*
> *"Blood that is spilled does not return to the body."*

---

### Meaning

The Odu of blood and consequence — sacrifice, warning, and the price of action.

### Associated Òrìṣà

Ṣàngó / Ọya

### Life Lesson

Ìrosùn warns that actions have irreversible consequences, and that ẹbọ (sacrifice) — whether of time, pride, or resources — is often required to avert disaster. It teaches accountability.

### Overview

Ìrosùn Méjì is linked with the colour red, with blood, and with the deep ties between the living and their lineage. Its tone is serious. It is often treated as a figure of warning, because it points to the weight of actions and the need to respond to them responsibly.

### Core Themes

- Accountability and consequence
- Ẹbọ (offering) as a way of restoring balance
- Lineage, family blood and inheritance
- Caution in anger and in haste

### Everyday Guidance

Tradition reads this figure as a call to slow down and take stock before acting, especially when emotions run high. Where harm has been done, it points toward repair: acknowledging it, making amends, and not repeating it.

### Reflection

Which of my actions still needs to be answered for or repaired?

### In the Wider System

title: Ọ̀wọ́nrín Méjì
theme: instability, change, the trickster's lesson, humility
proverb_yo: Ohun tó dúró jẹ́ẹ́, ni yíò yí padà.
proverb_en: What stands firm today may be overturned tomorrow.
excerpt: The Odu of upheaval and change — nothing stays the same, and pride
content:
## Ọ̀wọ́nrín Méjì

> *"Ohun tó dúró jẹ́ẹ́, ni yíò yí padà."*
> *"What stands firm today may be overturned tomorrow."*

---

### Meaning

The Odu of upheaval and change — nothing stays the same, and pride precedes a fall.

### Associated Òrìṣà

Èṣù / Ọ̀rúnmìlà

### Life Lesson

Ọ̀wọ́nrín teaches humility in success and resilience in reversal. It reminds us that fortunes change, so one must remain adaptable, avoid arrogance, and treat others well on the way up.

### Overview

Ọ̀wọ́nrín Méjì is associated with shifting situations, with chance, and with the trickster qualities attributed to Èṣù. Its pattern is unbalanced in a way that suggests instability, and its teaching is mostly about how to behave when circumstances turn.

### Core Themes

- Humility in success
- Resilience in reversal
- Adaptability and quick thinking
- Treating people well because fortunes change

### Everyday Guidance

This figure suggests that a position held today can change tomorrow, so kindness and good relationships are better security than status. It also advises preparing for uncertainty rather than pretending it will not come.

### Reflection

Am I treating people the way I would want to be treated if my position changed?

### In the Wider System

title: Ọ̀bàrà Méjì
theme: honour, boastfulness, the danger of pride, leadership
proverb_yo: Ìgbéraga ni í tẹ̀lé àṣejù ìṣọ́ra.
proverb_en: Excess confidence is often followed by a fall.
excerpt: The Odu of honour and pride — the gift and the danger of confidence.
content:
## Ọ̀bàrà Méjì

> *"Ìgbéraga ni í tẹ̀lé àṣejù ìṣọ́ra."*
> *"Excess confidence is often followed by a fall."*

---

### Meaning

The Odu of honour and pride — the gift and the danger of confidence.

### Associated Òrìṣà

Ṣàngó / Ọ̀bàtálá

### Life Lesson

Ọ̀bàrà teaches that leadership and confidence are gifts, but boastfulness invites downfall. True honour is shown through humility and generosity, not empty declarations.

### Overview

Ọ̀bàrà Méjì is connected with confidence, public standing and leadership. It treats these as real strengths that need guarding against their most common weakness, which is boastfulness. A person who speaks beyond what they have done invites a fall.

### Core Themes

- Leadership and public responsibility
- Pride and its consequences
- Generosity as proof of real honour
- Keeping promises and commitments

### Everyday Guidance

Read practically, this figure advises that a person should let results speak. Say less than you can do, deliver what you say, and share credit. Reputation built that way is stronger than one built on announcements.

### Reflection

Do my actions match what I say about myself?

### In the Wider System

theme: conflict, truth-telling, sharp consequences
proverb_yo: Òtítọ́ máa ń dùn, ṣùgbọ́n irọ́ máa ń pa ni níkẹyìn.
proverb_en: Truth may sting, but a lie eventually destroys.
excerpt: The Odu of sharp truths — conflict, exposure, and the cost of dishonesty.
content:
## Ọ̀kànràn Méjì

> *"Òtítọ́ máa ń dùn, ṣùgbọ́n irọ́ máa ń pa ni níkẹyìn."*
> *"Truth may sting, but a lie eventually destroys."*

---

### Meaning

The Odu of sharp truths — conflict, exposure, and the cost of dishonesty.

### Associated Òrìṣà

Ọya / Ògún

### Life Lesson

Ọ̀kànràn exposes what is hidden and warns against betrayal, gossip, and dishonesty. It teaches that confronting conflict honestly, though painful, prevents greater harm later.

### Overview

Ọ̀kànràn Méjì is tied to sharp speech, conflict and the exposure of what has been concealed. It is a figure of direct truth. The tradition connects it to the cost of lies, gossip and betrayal, and to the relief that comes when matters are faced openly.

### Core Themes

- Truthfulness even when uncomfortable
- The harm done by gossip and betrayal
- Confronting conflict early
- Careful use of words

### Everyday Guidance

In everyday terms, this figure advises resolving disputes directly rather than letting them grow in silence. It also asks a person to think before speaking, because words once said cannot be taken back.

### Reflection

Is there a conversation I have been avoiding that would clear the air?

title: Ògúndá Méjì
theme: struggle, tools, perseverance, clearing the path
proverb_yo: Ọ̀nà tí a kò gbóná, a kì í rìn án láìsí ọgbọ́n.
proverb_en: A path that has not been cleared cannot be walked without skill and effort.
excerpt: The Odu of struggle and perseverance — clearing a path through hardship
content:
## Ògúndá Méjì

> *"Ọ̀nà tí a kò gbóná, a kì í rìn án láìsí ọgbọ́n."*
> *"A path that has not been cleared cannot be walked without skill and effort."*

---

### Meaning

The Odu of struggle and perseverance — clearing a path through hardship with the tools you have.

### Associated Òrìṣà

Ògún

### Life Lesson

Ògúndá honours the warrior spirit of Ògún — perseverance, the courage to clear obstacles, and the discipline of using one's tools and skills wisely rather than recklessly.

### Overview

Ògúndá Méjì is associated with Ògún, the òrìṣà of iron, tools and the clearing of paths. Its themes are work, skill and perseverance. It honours the person who removes obstacles through effort and craft, and warns against using that same force carelessly.

### Core Themes

- Hard work and craftsmanship
- Clearing obstacles and opening roads
- Courage with discipline
- Responsible use of strength and tools

### Everyday Guidance

This figure reads as encouragement to keep working at a difficult task and to prepare the right tools before starting. It also cautions that power without restraint becomes destructive, so strength should be directed by purpose.

### Reflection

What obstacle am I ready to clear, and do I have the right tools?

title: Ọ̀sá Méjì
theme: upheaval, the whirlwind, sudden change, protection from harm
proverb_yo: Afẹ́fẹ́ tó le kì í fi ìgi sílẹ̀ láìṣí àyípadà.
proverb_en: A strong wind never leaves a tree unchanged.
excerpt: The Odu of the whirlwind — sudden upheaval that clears away stagnation.
content:
## Ọ̀sá Méjì

> *"Afẹ́fẹ́ tó le kì í fi ìgi sílẹ̀ láìṣí àyípadà."*
> *"A strong wind never leaves a tree unchanged."*

---

### Meaning

The Odu of the whirlwind — sudden upheaval that clears away stagnation.

### Associated Òrìṣà

Ọya

### Life Lesson

Ọ̀sá teaches resilience through sudden disruption. What feels destructive can also clear away what no longer serves growth. It calls for protection (ẹbọ) and steady faith during turbulent seasons.

### Overview

Ọ̀sá Méjì is linked with wind, sudden movement and upheaval. It describes events that arrive quickly and rearrange things. The tradition does not treat this only as danger. A storm can also remove what has become stale and make room for new growth.

### Core Themes

- Sudden change and how to meet it
- Protection through offerings and prayer
- Letting go of what cannot be held
- Steadiness during turbulence

### Everyday Guidance

Practically, this figure advises preparation and calm. Keep essentials secure, avoid reacting to every disturbance, and look for what the change makes possible once it settles.

### Reflection

What would I lose, and what might I gain, if things changed suddenly?

### In the Wider System

theme: cruelty, resentment, the need for restraint

proverb_en: A cruel heart never brings peace.
excerpt: The Odu that warns against cruelty, resentment, and the corrosive
content:
## Ìká Méjì

> *"Ìkà ọkàn kì í mú àlàáfíà wá."*
> *"A cruel heart never brings peace."*

---

### Meaning

The Odu that warns against cruelty, resentment, and the corrosive effects of malice.

### Associated Òrìṣà

Ọya / Èṣù

### Life Lesson

Ìká warns of the dangers of bitterness, envy, and vengeance — both suffering it and inflicting it. It teaches restraint, forgiveness, and guarding one's heart against becoming hardened by pain.

### Overview

Ìká Méjì is concerned with the inner life of bitterness, envy and cruelty, both in oneself and in others. It is a moral figure. Its attention is on how unresolved pain can harden into harmful behaviour, and on the self-control needed to prevent that.

### Core Themes

- Restraint and self-mastery
- Forgiveness as protection for oneself
- Recognising envy and resentment
- Not repaying harm with harm

### Everyday Guidance

This figure counsels watchfulness over one's own heart. If someone has wronged you, address it but do not let it define you. It also advises caution around people whose behaviour is driven by resentment.

### Reflection

Which old hurt am I still feeding?

title: Òtúrúpọ̀n Méjì
theme: illness and healing, secrets of the body, patience
proverb_yo: Àrùn tí a kò tọ́jú lọ́nà tí ó tọ́ kì í yá.
proverb_en: An illness not treated in the right way does not heal.
excerpt: The Odu of illness and healing — patience with the body and the wisdom
content:
## Òtúrúpọ̀n Méjì

> *"Àrùn tí a kò tọ́jú lọ́nà tí ó tọ́ kì í yá."*
> *"An illness not treated in the right way does not heal."*

---

### Meaning

The Odu of illness and healing — patience with the body and the wisdom of proper treatment.

### Associated Òrìṣà

Ọbàtálá / Ọ̀rúnmìlà

### Life Lesson

Òtúrúpọ̀n calls for patience, proper diagnosis before action, and respect for the body's natural healing processes. It also symbolises the wisdom that comes from surviving hardship.

### Overview

Òtúrúpọ̀n Méjì is associated with illness, recovery and the body. In the tradition's reading, health is something to understand carefully, not to rush. The figure also stands for the strength of those who have come through hardship.

### Core Themes

- Proper diagnosis before action
- Patience in healing
- Respect for the body and its limits
- Wisdom gained from surviving difficulty

### Everyday Guidance

Read in daily life, this figure advises seeking the right help early, following treatment through, and resting enough. It also encourages care for people who are unwell, since recovery is helped by support.

### Reflection

Am I paying attention to what my body and mind are telling me?

title: Òtúrá Méjì
theme: transformation, clarity after confusion, truth revealed
proverb_yo: Kùràkùrà ọjọ́ ni ìmọ́lẹ̀ ọjọ́ tuntun.
proverb_en: The dimness before dawn gives way to the light of a new day.
excerpt: The Odu of transformation — clarity and truth emerging after a period
content:
## Òtúrá Méjì

> *"Kùràkùrà ọjọ́ ni ìmọ́lẹ̀ ọjọ́ tuntun."*
> *"The dimness before dawn gives way to the light of a new day."*

---

### Meaning

The Odu of transformation — clarity and truth emerging after a period of confusion.

### Associated Òrìṣà

Ọ̀rúnmìlà / Ọbàtálá

### Life Lesson

Òtúrá teaches that confusion and difficulty are often temporary, giving way to clarity for those who remain patient and truthful. It marks turning points and the wisdom gained through transformation.

### Overview

Òtúrá Méjì marks a turn from confusion to clarity. Its pattern and name are associated with peace, with speaking truthfully, and with the moment when a problem becomes understandable. It carries a calmer tone than some of the more cautionary figures.

### Core Themes

- Clarity after difficulty
- Peaceful speech and reconciliation
- Turning points and transformation
- Patience until understanding arrives

### Everyday Guidance

In practice, the figure encourages a person not to make final decisions in the middle of confusion. Wait for understanding, speak calmly, and expect that the picture will clear for those who stay honest and patient.

### Reflection

What decision should wait until I can see more clearly?

title: Ìrẹtẹ̀ Méjì
theme: perseverance despite setbacks, hidden victory
proverb_yo: Ìṣẹ́gun tí a kò fojú rí ni í dùn jù.
proverb_en: The victory unseen by others is often the sweetest.
excerpt: The Odu of quiet perseverance — victory that comes after private struggle.
content:
## Ìrẹtẹ̀ Méjì

> *"Ìṣẹ́gun tí a kò fojú rí ni í dùn jù."*
> *"The victory unseen by others is often the sweetest."*

---

### Meaning

The Odu of quiet perseverance — victory that comes after private struggle.

### Associated Òrìṣà

Ọ̀rúnmìlà / Ọya

### Life Lesson

Ìrẹtẹ̀ teaches resilience in adversity, especially struggles others cannot see. It reassures that persistence — even quiet, unglamorous effort — leads to eventual triumph.

### Overview

Ìrẹtẹ̀ Méjì is associated with persistence through setbacks and with achievements that others do not see. It is a figure for people doing steady work without recognition, and it treats that quiet effort as meaningful in itself.

### Core Themes

- Perseverance in the face of delay
- Private effort that leads to later success
- Not being discouraged by comparison
- Careful, patient progress

### Everyday Guidance

This figure reads as reassurance for those who feel stuck. Keep going, keep records of progress, and avoid measuring yourself against people whose circumstances differ. Results often arrive later than hoped but are lasting when earned.

### Reflection

What am I building quietly that deserves more patience?

## Ọ̀ṣẹ́ Méjì

> *"Ọwọ́ tí ó fúnni, ni Ọlọ́run í fi kún."*
> *"The hand that gives is the one Olódùmarè fills."*

---

### Meaning

The Odu of blessings and sweetness — abundance that flows from generosity and gratitude.

### Associated Òrìṣà

Ọ̀ṣun

### Life Lesson

Ọ̀ṣẹ́ celebrates the sweetness of life earned through generosity, hospitality, and gratitude. It teaches that abundance flows to those who share freely and honour Ọ̀ṣun's spirit of grace.

### Overview

Ọ̀ṣẹ́ Méjì is linked with Ọ̀ṣun and with sweetness, beauty, abundance and care. It speaks of prosperity that comes through generosity and good relationships rather than through hoarding.

### Core Themes

- Gratitude and hospitality
- Generosity as the root of abundance
- Beauty, care and attractiveness of character
- Healthy relationships and community

### Everyday Guidance

Practically, this figure suggests giving freely where one can, expressing thanks, and keeping a warm home and workplace. It also reminds a person that sweetness is not weakness, and that kindness takes discipline.

### Reflection

Who can I support or thank this week?

### In the Wider System

This is a principal figure (Odù Méjì). It is the first parent of 15 of the 240 compound figures (Omo Odù), and the second parent of another 15. Each of those inherits something of this figure's character and adds the influence of its partner.

*This page is an interpretive summary written for general readers. Practising priests (babaláwo) hold the full oral corpus (ẹsẹ Ifá) for each Odù, which is learned through apprenticeship and is not reproduced here.*

---

excerpt: The elder Odu of purity and completion — moral integrity across a long life.
content:
## Òfún Méjì

> *"Funfun ni àrà; kò gba ìdọ̀tí láti dúró funfun."*
> *"White is sacred; it takes discipline to remain unstained."*

---

### Meaning

The elder Odu of purity and completion — moral integrity across a long life.

### Associated Òrìṣà

Ọbàtálá / Olódùmarè

### Life Lesson

Òfún, closely tied to Ọbàtálá, teaches purity of character, patience, and the moral discipline required to age gracefully and finish life's journey with integrity intact.

### Overview

Òfún Méjì is associated with Ọbàtálá, with whiteness, purity and calm authority. It is often read as a figure of completion and moral integrity, and it connects with the dignity of old age and a life lived with care.

### Core Themes

- Purity of character and intention
- Calm, patient authority
- Completion and finishing well
- Respect for elders and for ritual discipline

### Everyday Guidance

In daily terms, this figure advises keeping one's word, being slow to anger, and finishing what one starts. It is also a reminder that integrity is maintained through small choices made consistently.

### Reflection

What would it mean to finish this chapter of my life with integrity?

excerpt: Light meets the threshold of the ancestors. This figure speaks of a bright beginning that must be built on respect for those who came before, and of potential that is only realised when it is rooted in lineage.
content:
## Ogbè-Ọ̀yẹ̀kú

### Overview

Light meets the threshold of the ancestors. This figure speaks of a bright beginning that must be built on respect for those who came before, and of potential that is only realised when it is rooted in lineage.

### Governing Influences

* **Èjì Ogbè** — light, new beginnings, divine potential (Ọ̀rúnmìlà / Olódùmarè)
* **Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Méjì** — endings, the ancestors, the unseen world, mortality (Ikú (Death) / Ọ̀sun)


### Guidance

Honour your ancestors before launching a new venture, and let gratitude steady your ambition.

<!-- READING_START -->

### How this figure is read

In Ifá, a figure is built from two columns of four marks, read from the right column to the left. Here the right column is Èjì Ogbè (single · single · single · single) and the left column is Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Méjì (double · double · double · double). Many diviners start with the right column and then bring in the left, though schools of Ifá differ in how they weigh the two. Reading Ogbè-Ọ̀yẹ̀kú means holding both lessons together and asking how they bear on the question at hand.

### From Èjì Ogbè

You were not born by accident. Every person carries an ori (destiny) chosen before birth. Ogbè teaches that your task is to remember and fulfil your purpose, and to lead with clarity, honesty and generosity of spirit.

*Imọ́lẹ̀ kìí ṣe n̄ǹkan tí a fún ọ — imọ́lẹ̀ ni ọ jẹ́.*  
"Light is not something given to you — light is what you are."

### From Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Méjì

Ọ̀yẹ̀kú teaches respect for the ancestors, acceptance of mortality, and the understanding that every ending clears space for renewal. It warns against arrogance in the face of life's fragility.

*Òkú tó sun, kì í jí mọ́; ẹ̀mí tó lọ, kì í padà bí ara.*  
"The dead that sleeps does not wake again; the spirit that departs does not return in the same body."

### Putting the two together

When this figure is cast, tradition reads it as encouragement to act openly. Plan in the light, speak plainly, and avoid shortcuts that need to be hidden later. It also reminds a person that a good start still needs steady follow-through. At the same time, read in daily life, this figure asks a person to honour those who came before, settle unfinished obligations, and stop treating limits as enemies. It cautions against pride about health, wealth or status, since all of them are borrowed for a time.

Interpretations of individual Omo Odù differ between lineages and between diviners, so treat this page as a reading aid and not a ruling. A consultation with a trained Babaláwo or Ìyánífá will always be fuller than any written summary.

<!-- READING_END -->

- - -

*Ogbè-Ọ̀yẹ̀kú is one of the 240 Omo Odù formed by combining two of the 16 principal Odù Méjì. Naming conventions for Omo Odù can vary between Ifá lineages; this entry uses a systematic right–left naming for clarity.*

## Ogbè-Ìwòrì

### Overview

Clarity of purpose joins deep self-knowledge. The success you seek is already in you, but you must look honestly inward to find where it is hidden.

### Governing Influences

* **Èjì Ogbè** — light, new beginnings, divine potential (Ọ̀rúnmìlà / Olódùmarè)
* **Ìwòrì Méjì** — self-knowledge, hidden truth, inner vision (Ọ̀sanyìn / Ọ̀rúnmìlà)


### Guidance

Spend time in reflection before acting. Seek truth about yourself first and the way outward will open.

<!-- READING_START -->

### How this figure is read

In Ifá, a figure is built from two columns of four marks, read from the right column to the left. Here the right column is Èjì Ogbè (single · single · single · single) and the left column is Ìwòrì Méjì (double · single · single · double). Many diviners start with the right column and then bring in the left, though schools of Ifá differ in how they weigh the two. Reading Ogbè-Ìwòrì means holding both lessons together and asking how they bear on the question at hand.

### From Èjì Ogbè

You were not born by accident. Every person carries an ori (destiny) chosen before birth. Ogbè teaches that your task is to remember and fulfil your purpose, and to lead with clarity, honesty and generosity of spirit.

*Imọ́lẹ̀ kìí ṣe n̄ǹkan tí a fún ọ — imọ́lẹ̀ ni ọ jẹ́.*  
"Light is not something given to you — light is what you are."

### From Ìwòrì Méjì

Ìwòrì calls for introspection and honesty about one's own motives before judging others. It reveals secrets — both dangerous and beneficial — and teaches that true wisdom begins with self-awareness.

*Bí a kò bá mọ ara ẹni, a kì í mọ ẹlòmíràn.*  
"If one does not know oneself, one cannot truly know another."

### Putting the two together

When this figure is cast, tradition reads it as encouragement to act openly. Plan in the light, speak plainly, and avoid shortcuts that need to be hidden later. It also reminds a person that a good start still needs steady follow-through. At the same time, tradition uses this figure to counsel reflection. Before blaming, ask what part is yours. Before trusting a story, look for what is missing from it. Insight gained this way can protect a person from deception, including self-deception.

Interpretations of individual Omo Odù differ between lineages and between diviners, so treat this page as a reading aid and not a ruling. A consultation with a trained Babaláwo or Ìyánífá will always be fuller than any written summary.

<!-- READING_END -->

*Ogbè-Ìwòrì is one of the 240 Omo Odù formed by combining two of the 16 principal Odù Méjì. Naming conventions for Omo Odù can vary between Ifá lineages; this entry uses a systematic right–left naming for clarity.*

title: Ogbè-Òdí
theme: light, new beginnings, divine potential; the womb, mystery,
excerpt: Open possibility enters a closed, mysterious space. Something promising is gestating and cannot be hurried; the light is present even where it is not yet visible.
content:
## Ogbè-Òdí

### Overview

Open possibility enters a closed, mysterious space. Something promising is gestating and cannot be hurried; the light is present even where it is not yet visible.

### Governing Influences

* **Èjì Ogbè** — light, new beginnings, divine potential (Ọ̀rúnmìlà / Olódùmarè)
* **Òdí Méjì** — the womb, mystery, transformation, hidden depth (Ọya / Yemọja)


### Guidance

Be patient with projects still taking shape and protect them from premature exposure.

<!-- READING_START -->

### How this figure is read

In Ifá, a figure is built from two columns of four marks, read from the right column to the left. Here the right column is Èjì Ogbè (single · single · single · single) and the left column is Òdí Méjì (single · double · double · single). Many diviners start with the right column and then bring in the left, though schools of Ifá differ in how they weigh the two. Reading Ogbè-Òdí means holding both lessons together and asking how they bear on the question at hand.

### From Èjì Ogbè

You were not born by accident. Every person carries an ori (destiny) chosen before birth. Ogbè teaches that your task is to remember and fulfil your purpose, and to lead with clarity, honesty and generosity of spirit.

*Imọ́lẹ̀ kìí ṣe n̄ǹkan tí a fún ọ — imọ́lẹ̀ ni ọ jẹ́.*  
"Light is not something given to you — light is what you are."

### From Òdí Méjì

Òdí teaches patience with processes that are not yet visible — pregnancy, growth, and transformation take time in darkness before they emerge into light. It also warns against forcing what must unfold naturally.

*Ohun tó wà nínú, kì í fi ara rẹ̀ hàn ní ọ̀nà kan ṣoṣo.*  
"What is within does not reveal itself in only one way."

### Putting the two together

When this figure is cast, tradition reads it as encouragement to act openly. Plan in the light, speak plainly, and avoid shortcuts that need to be hidden later. It also reminds a person that a good start still needs steady follow-through. At the same time, in practice, this figure advises a person not to uncover a plan, a project or a relationship too early. Give it time and shelter. It also warns against forcing outcomes, because pressure applied at the wrong stage can damage what is forming.

Interpretations of individual Omo Odù differ between lineages and between diviners, so treat this page as a reading aid and not a ruling. A consultation with a trained Babaláwo or Ìyánífá will always be fuller than any written summary.

<!-- READING_END -->

- - -

*Ogbè-Òdí is one of the 240 Omo Odù formed by combining two of the 16 principal Odù Méjì. Naming conventions for Omo Odù can vary between Ifá lineages; this entry uses a systematic right–left naming for clarity.*

title: Ogbè-Ìrosùn

excerpt: Divine favour is tied to sacrifice. Blessings are available, but they follow a willingness to give something up and to keep promises made to the Òrìṣà.
content:
## Ogbè-Ìrosùn

### Overview

Divine favour is tied to sacrifice. Blessings are available, but they follow a willingness to give something up and to keep promises made to the Òrìṣà.

### Governing Influences

* **Èjì Ogbè** — light, new beginnings, divine potential (Ọ̀rúnmìlà / Olódùmarè)
* **Ìrosùn Méjì** — blood, sacrifice, warning, consequence (Ṣàngó / Ọya)


### Guidance

Make the offering or commitment you have been postponing, and keep your word.

<!-- READING_START -->

### How this figure is read

In Ifá, a figure is built from two columns of four marks, read from the right column to the left. Here the right column is Èjì Ogbè (single · single · single · single) and the left column is Ìrosùn Méjì (single · single · double · double). Many diviners start with the right column and then bring in the left, though schools of Ifá differ in how they weigh the two. Reading Ogbè-Ìrosùn means holding both lessons together and asking how they bear on the question at hand.

### From Èjì Ogbè

You were not born by accident. Every person carries an ori (destiny) chosen before birth. Ogbè teaches that your task is to remember and fulfil your purpose, and to lead with clarity, honesty and generosity of spirit.

*Imọ́lẹ̀ kìí ṣe n̄ǹkan tí a fún ọ — imọ́lẹ̀ ni ọ jẹ́.*  
"Light is not something given to you — light is what you are."

### From Ìrosùn Méjì

Ìrosùn warns that actions have irreversible consequences, and that ẹbọ (sacrifice) — whether of time, pride, or resources — is often required to avert disaster. It teaches accountability.

*Ẹ̀jẹ̀ tí a tú sílẹ̀ kì í padà sí inú ara.*  
"Blood that is spilled does not return to the body."

### Putting the two together

When this figure is cast, tradition reads it as encouragement to act openly. Plan in the light, speak plainly, and avoid shortcuts that need to be hidden later. It also reminds a person that a good start still needs steady follow-through. At the same time, tradition reads this figure as a call to slow down and take stock before acting, especially when emotions run high. Where harm has been done, it points toward repair: acknowledging it, making amends, and not repeating it.

Interpretations of individual Omo Odù differ between lineages and between diviners, so treat this page as a reading aid and not a ruling. A consultation with a trained Babaláwo or Ìyánífá will always be fuller than any written summary.

<!-- READING_END -->

- - -

*Ogbè-Ìrosùn is one of the 240 Omo Odù formed by combining two of the 16 principal Odù Méjì. Naming conventions for Omo Odù can vary between Ifá lineages; this entry uses a systematic right–left naming for clarity.*

Fortune is bright but unstable. The caution is that good luck can turn quickly, and humility is what keeps a blessing in place.

### Governing Influences

* **Èjì Ogbè** — light, new beginnings, divine potential (Ọ̀rúnmìlà / Olódùmarè)
* **Ọ̀wọ́nrín Méjì** — instability, change, the trickster's lesson, humility (Èṣù / Ọ̀rúnmìlà)


### Guidance

Stay modest in success and prepare for changing circumstances.

## Ogbè-Ọ̀bàrà

### Overview

Natural leadership is tested by pride. It grants honour and standing, then asks whether you can carry them without boasting.

### Governing Influences

* **Ogbè** — light, new beginnings, divine potential (Ọ̀rúnmìlà / Olódùmarè)
* **Ọ̀bàrà Méjì** — honour, boastfulness, the danger of pride, leadership (Ṣàngó / Ọ̀bàtálá)


### Guidance

Lead by example, speak less of your achievements, and let your work speak for you.

<!-- READING_START -->

### How this figure is read

In Ifá, a figure is built from two columns of four marks, read from the right column to the left. Here the right column is Èjì Ogbè (single · single · single · single) and the left column is Ọ̀bàrà Méjì (single · double · double · double). Many diviners start with the right column and then bring in the left, though schools of Ifá differ in how they weigh the two. Reading Ogbè-Ọ̀bàrà means holding both lessons together and asking how they bear on the question at hand.

### From Èjì Ogbè

You were not born by accident. Every person carries an ori (destiny) chosen before birth. Ogbè teaches that your task is to remember and fulfil your purpose, and to lead with clarity, honesty and generosity of spirit.

*Imọ́lẹ̀ kìí ṣe n̄ǹkan tí a fún ọ — imọ́lẹ̀ ni ọ jẹ́.*  
"Light is not something given to you — light is what you are."

### From Ọ̀bàrà Méjì

Ọ̀bàrà teaches that leadership and confidence are gifts, but boastfulness invites downfall. True honour is shown through humility and generosity, not empty declarations.

*Ìgbéraga ni í tẹ̀lé àṣejù ìṣọ́ra.*  
"Excess confidence is often followed by a fall."

### Putting the two together

When this figure is cast, tradition reads it as encouragement to act openly. Plan in the light, speak plainly, and avoid shortcuts that need to be hidden later. It also reminds a person that a good start still needs steady follow-through. At the same time, read practically, this figure advises that a person should let results speak. Say less than you can do, deliver what you say, and share credit. Reputation built that way is stronger than one built on announcements.

Interpretations of individual Omo Odù differ between lineages and between diviners, so treat this page as a reading aid and not a ruling. A consultation with a trained Babaláwo or Ìyánífá will always be fuller than any written summary.

## Ogbè-Ọ̀kànràn

### Overview

Truth is spoken into a heated situation. Light exposes what is wrong, and can cause conflict before it brings peace.

### Governing Influences

* **Èjì Ogbè** — light, new beginnings, divine potential (Ọ̀rúnmìlà / Olódùmarè)
* **Ọ̀kànràn Méjì** — conflict, truth-telling, sharp consequences (Ọya / Ògún)


### Guidance

Say what must be said with care, and avoid answering anger with anger.

<!-- READING_START -->

### How this figure is read

In Ifá, a figure is built from two columns of four marks, read from the right column to the left. Here the right column is Èjì Ogbè (single · single · single · single) and the left column is Ọ̀kànràn Méjì (double · double · double · single). Many diviners start with the right column and then bring in the left, though schools of Ifá differ in how they weigh the two. ### From Èjì Ogbè

*Imọ́lẹ̀ kìí ṣe n̄ǹkan tí a fún ọ — imọ́lẹ̀ ni ọ jẹ́.*  
"Light is not something given to you — light is what you are."

### From Ọ̀kànràn Méjì

Ọ̀kànràn exposes what is hidden and warns against betrayal, gossip, and dishonesty. It teaches that confronting conflict honestly, though painful, prevents greater harm later.

*Òtítọ́ máa ń dùn, ṣùgbọ́n irọ́ máa ń pa ni níkẹyìn.*  
"Truth may sting, but a lie eventually destroys."

### Putting the two together

When this figure is cast, tradition reads it as encouragement to act openly. Plan in the light, speak plainly, and avoid shortcuts that need to be hidden later. It also reminds a person that a good start still needs steady follow-through. At the same time, in everyday terms, this figure advises resolving disputes directly rather than letting them grow in silence. It also asks a person to think before speaking, because words once said cannot be taken back.

Interpretations of individual Omo Odù differ between lineages and between diviners, so treat this page as a reading aid and not a ruling. A consultation with a trained Babaláwo or Ìyánífá will always be fuller than any written summary.

## Ogbè-Ògúndá

### Overview

Opportunity arrives with hard work attached. The way forward is open, but it must be cleared by effort, skill and perseverance.

### Governing Influences

* **Èjì Ogbè** — light, new beginnings, divine potential (Ọ̀rúnmìlà / Olódùmarè)
* **Ògúndá Méjì** — struggle, tools, perseverance, clearing the path (Ògún)


### Guidance

Take up your tools and work steadily; the path will respond to determination.

<!-- READING_START -->

### How this figure is read

In Ifá, a figure is built from two columns of four marks, read from the right column to the left. Here the right column is Èjì Ogbè (single · single · single · single) and the left column is Ògúndá Méjì (single · single · single · double). Many diviners start with the right column and then bring in the left, though schools of Ifá differ in how they weigh the two. Reading Ogbè-Ògúndá means holding both lessons together and asking how they bear on the question at hand.

### From Èjì Ogbè

You were not born by accident. Every person carries an ori (destiny) chosen before birth. Ogbè teaches that your task is to remember and fulfil your purpose, and to lead with clarity, honesty and generosity of spirit.

*Imọ́lẹ̀ kìí ṣe n̄ǹkan tí a fún ọ — imọ́lẹ̀ ni ọ jẹ́.*  
"Light is not something given to you — light is what you are."

### From Ògúndá Méjì

Ògúndá honours the warrior spirit of Ògún — perseverance, the courage to clear obstacles, and the discipline of using one's tools and skills wisely rather than recklessly.

*Ọ̀nà tí a kò gbóná, a kì í rìn án láìsí ọgbọ́n.*  
"A path that has not been cleared cannot be walked without skill and effort."

### Putting the two together

When this figure is cast, tradition reads it as encouragement to act openly. Plan in the light, speak plainly, and avoid shortcuts that need to be hidden later. It also reminds a person that a good start still needs steady follow-through. At the same time, this figure reads as encouragement to keep working at a difficult task and to prepare the right tools before starting. It also cautions that power without restraint becomes destructive, so strength should be directed by purpose.

Interpretations of individual Omo Odù differ between lineages and between diviners, so treat this page as a reading aid and not a ruling. A consultation with a trained Babaláwo or Ìyánífá will always be fuller than any written summary.

* **Èjì Ogbè** — light, new beginnings, divine potential (Ọ̀rúnmìlà / Olódùmarè)
* **Ọ̀sá Méjì** — upheaval, the whirlwind, sudden change, protection from harm (Ọya)

A bright path crosses a whirlwind. Sudden change threatens plans, yet the figure promises protection to those who stay grounded.

Governing Influences

* Èjì Ogbè — light, new beginnings, divine potential (Ọ̀rúnmìlà / Olódùmarè) * Ọ̀sá Méjì — upheaval, the whirlwind, sudden change, protection from harm (Ọya)

Guidance

Expect disruption, keep your counsel, and hold on to your principles while things settle.

How this figure is read

In Ifá, a figure is built from two columns of four marks, read from the right column to the left. Here the right column is Èjì Ogbè (single · single · single · single) and the left column is Ọ̀sá Méjì (double · single · single · single). Many diviners start with the right column and then bring in the left, though schools of Ifá differ in how they weigh the two. Reading Ogbè-Ọ̀sá means holding both lessons together and asking how they bear on the question at hand.

From Èjì Ogbè

You were not born by accident. Every person carries an ori (destiny) chosen before birth. Ogbè teaches that your task is to remember and fulfil your purpose, and to lead with clarity, honesty and generosity of spirit.

Imọ́lẹ̀ kìí ṣe n̄ǹkan tí a fún ọ — imọ́lẹ̀ ni ọ jẹ́. "Light is not something given to you — light is what you are."

From Ọ̀sá Méjì

Ọ̀sá teaches resilience through sudden disruption. What feels destructive can also clear away what no longer serves growth. It calls for protection (ẹbọ) and steady faith during turbulent seasons.

Afẹ́fẹ́ tó le kì í fi ìgi sílẹ̀ láìṣí àyípadà. "A strong wind never leaves a tree unchanged."

Putting the two together

When this figure is cast, tradition reads it as encouragement to act openly. Plan in the light, speak plainly, and avoid shortcuts that need to be hidden later. It also reminds a person that a good start still needs steady follow-through. At the same time, practically, this figure advises preparation and calm. Keep essentials secure, avoid reacting to every disturbance, and look for what the change makes possible once it settles.

Interpretations of individual Omo Odù differ between lineages and between diviners, so treat this page as a reading aid and not a ruling. A consultation with a trained Babaláwo or Ìyánífá will always be fuller than any written summary.

## Ogbè-Òtúrúpọ̀n

### Overview

It joins vitality with the call to heal. Good fortune depends on caring for the body and being patient with slow recovery.

### Governing Influences

* **Èjì Ogbè** — light, new beginnings, divine potential (Ọ̀rúnmìlà / Olódùmarè)
* **Òtúrúpọ̀n Méjì** — illness and healing, secrets of the body, patience (Ọbàtálá / Ọ̀rúnmìlà)


### Guidance

Attend to your health, seek proper treatment, and give healing the time it needs.

<!-- READING_START -->

### How this figure is read

In Ifá, a figure is built from two columns of four marks, read from the right column to the left. Here the right column is Èjì Ogbè (single · single · single · single) and the left column is Òtúrúpọ̀n Méjì (double · double · single · double). Many diviners start with the right column and then bring in the left, though schools of Ifá differ in how they weigh the two. Reading Ogbè-Òtúrúpọ̀n means holding both lessons together and asking how they bear on the question at hand.

### From Èjì Ogbè

You were not born by accident. Every person carries an ori (destiny) chosen before birth. Ogbè teaches that your task is to remember and fulfil your purpose, and to lead with clarity, honesty and generosity of spirit.

*Imọ́lẹ̀ kìí ṣe n̄ǹkan tí a fún ọ — imọ́lẹ̀ ni ọ jẹ́.*  
"Light is not something given to you — light is what you are."

### From Òtúrúpọ̀n Méjì

Òtúrúpọ̀n calls for patience, proper diagnosis before action, and respect for the body's natural healing processes. It also symbolises the wisdom that comes from surviving hardship.

*Àrùn tí a kò tọ́jú lọ́nà tí ó tọ́ kì í yá.*  
"An illness not treated in the right way does not heal."

### Putting the two together

When this figure is cast, tradition reads it as encouragement to act openly. Plan in the light, speak plainly, and avoid shortcuts that need to be hidden later. It also reminds a person that a good start still needs steady follow-through. At the same time, read in daily life, this figure advises seeking the right help early, following treatment through, and resting enough. It also encourages care for people who are unwell, since recovery is helped by support.

Interpretations of individual Omo Odù differ between lineages and between diviners, so treat this page as a reading aid and not a ruling. A consultation with a trained Babaláwo or Ìyánífá will always be fuller than any written summary.

## Ogbè-Òtúrá

### Overview

Understanding follows a period of confusion. Truth that was hidden comes into view and brings a new sense of direction.

### Governing Influences

* **Èjì Ogbè** — light, new beginnings, divine potential (Ọ̀rúnmìlà / Olódùmarè)
* **Òtúrá Méjì** — transformation, clarity after confusion, truth revealed (Ọ̀rúnmìlà / Ọbàtálá)


### Guidance

Trust that answers are coming. Act once the picture is clear rather than in the fog.

<!-- READING_START -->

### How this figure is read

In Ifá, a figure is built from two columns of four marks, read from the right column to the left. Here the right column is Èjì Ogbè (single · single · single · single) and the left column is Òtúrá Méjì (single · double · single · single). Many diviners start with the right column and then bring in the left, though schools of Ifá differ in how they weigh the two. Reading Ogbè-Òtúrá means holding both lessons together and asking how they bear on the question at hand.

### From Èjì Ogbè

You were not born by accident. Every person carries an ori (destiny) chosen before birth. Ogbè teaches that your task is to remember and fulfil your purpose, and to lead with clarity, honesty and generosity of spirit.

*Imọ́lẹ̀ kìí ṣe n̄ǹkan tí a fún ọ — imọ́lẹ̀ ni ọ jẹ́.*  
"Light is not something given to you — light is what you are."

### From Òtúrá Méjì

Òtúrá teaches that confusion and difficulty are often temporary, giving way to clarity for those who remain patient and truthful. It marks turning points and the wisdom gained through transformation.

*Kùràkùrà ọjọ́ ni ìmọ́lẹ̀ ọjọ́ tuntun.*  
"The dimness before dawn gives way to the light of a new day."

### Putting the two together

When this figure is cast, tradition reads it as encouragement to act openly. Plan in the light, speak plainly, and avoid shortcuts that need to be hidden later. It also reminds a person that a good start still needs steady follow-through. At the same time, in practice, the figure encourages a person not to make final decisions in the middle of confusion. Wait for understanding, speak calmly, and expect that the picture will clear for those who stay honest and patient.

Interpretations of individual Omo Odù differ between lineages and between diviners, so treat this page as a reading aid and not a ruling. A consultation with a trained Babaláwo or Ìyánífá will always be fuller than any written summary.

## Ogbè-Ìrẹtẹ̀

### Overview

Success is delayed but not denied. A setback is only a stage; the figure confirms that persistence brings a hidden victory.

### Governing Influences

* **Èjì Ogbè** — light, new beginnings, divine potential (Ọ̀rúnmìlà / Olódùmarè)
* **Ìrẹtẹ̀ Méjì** — perseverance despite setbacks, hidden victory (Ọ̀rúnmìlà / Ọya)


### Guidance

Keep going through disappointment. Your effort is being rewarded in ways not yet visible.

<!-- READING_START -->

### How this figure is read

In Ifá, a figure is built from two columns of four marks, read from the right column to the left. Here the right column is Èjì Ogbè (single · single · single · single) and the left column is Ìrẹtẹ̀ Méjì (single · single · double · single). Many diviners start with the right column and then bring in the left, though schools of Ifá differ in how they weigh the two. You were not born by accident. Every person carries an ori (destiny) chosen before birth. Ogbè teaches that your task is to remember and fulfil your purpose, and to lead with clarity, honesty and generosity of spirit.

*Imọ́lẹ̀ kìí ṣe n̄ǹkan tí a fún ọ — imọ́lẹ̀ ni ọ jẹ́.*  
"Light is not something given to you — light is what you are."

### From Ìrẹtẹ̀ Méjì

Ìrẹtẹ̀ teaches resilience in adversity, especially struggles others cannot see. It reassures that persistence — even quiet, unglamorous effort — leads to eventual triumph.

*Ìṣẹ́gun tí a kò fojú rí ni í dùn jù.*  
"The victory unseen by others is often the sweetest."

### Putting the two together

When this figure is cast, tradition reads it as encouragement to act openly. Plan in the light, speak plainly, and avoid shortcuts that need to be hidden later. It also reminds a person that a good start still needs steady follow-through. At the same time, this figure reads as reassurance for those who feel stuck. Keep going, keep records of progress, and avoid measuring yourself against people whose circumstances differ. Results often arrive later than hoped but are lasting when earned.

Interpretations of individual Omo Odù differ between lineages and between diviners, so treat this page as a reading aid and not a ruling. A consultation with a trained Babaláwo or Ìyánífá will always be fuller than any written summary.

## Ogbè-Ọ̀ṣẹ́

### Overview

Abundance and gratitude walk together. It points to sweetness in life, and to a duty to share it generously.

### Governing Influences

* **Èjì Ogbè** — light, new beginnings, divine potential (Ọ̀rúnmìlà / Olódùmarè)
* **Ọ̀ṣẹ́ Méjì** — blessings, sweetness, abundance, gratitude (Ọ̀ṣun)


### Guidance

Give thanks openly and share your good fortune; generosity multiplies blessings.

<!-- READING_START -->

### How this figure is read

In Ifá, a figure is built from two columns of four marks, read from the right column to the left. Here the right column is Èjì Ogbè (single · single · single · single) and the left column is Ọ̀ṣẹ́ Méjì (single · double · single · double). "Light is not something given to you — light is what you are."

### From Ọ̀ṣẹ́ Méjì

Ọ̀ṣẹ́ celebrates the sweetness of life earned through generosity, hospitality, and gratitude. It teaches that abundance flows to those who share freely and honour Ọ̀ṣun's spirit of grace.

*Ọwọ́ tí ó fúnni, ni Ọlọ́run í fi kún.*  
"The hand that gives is the one Olódùmarè fills."

### Putting the two together

When this figure is cast, tradition reads it as encouragement to act openly. Plan in the light, speak plainly, and avoid shortcuts that need to be hidden later. It also reminds a person that a good start still needs steady follow-through. At the same time, practically, this figure suggests giving freely where one can, expressing thanks, and keeping a warm home and workplace. It also reminds a person that sweetness is not weakness, and that kindness takes discipline.

Abundance and gratitude walk together. It points to sweetness in life, and to a duty to share it generously.

Governing Influences

## Ọ̀yẹ̀kú-Ogbè

### Overview

The unseen world presses toward the light. The ancestors bring a message and ask that it be turned into a living, practical beginning.

### Governing Influences

* **Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Méjì** — endings, the ancestors, the unseen world, mortality (Ikú (Death) / Ọ̀sun)
* **Èjì Ogbè** — light, new beginnings, divine potential (Ọ̀rúnmìlà / Olódùmarè)


### Guidance

Listen for guidance from elders and ancestors, then act on it with confidence.

<!-- READING_START -->

### How this figure is read

In Ifá, a figure is built from two columns of four marks, read from the right column to the left. Here the right column is Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Méjì (double · double · double · double) and the left column is Èjì Ogbè (single · single · single · single). Many diviners start with the right column and then bring in the left, though schools of Ifá differ in how they weigh the two. Reading Ọ̀yẹ̀kú-Ogbè means holding both lessons together and asking how they bear on the question at hand.

### From Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Méjì

Ọ̀yẹ̀kú teaches respect for the ancestors, acceptance of mortality, and the understanding that every ending clears space for renewal. It warns against arrogance in the face of life's fragility.

*Òkú tó sun, kì í jí mọ́; ẹ̀mí tó lọ, kì í padà bí ara.*  
"The dead that sleeps does not wake again; the spirit that departs does not return in the same body."

### From Èjì Ogbè

You were not born by accident. Every person carries an ori (destiny) chosen before birth. Ogbè teaches that your task is to remember and fulfil your purpose, and to lead with clarity, honesty and generosity of spirit.

*Imọ́lẹ̀ kìí ṣe n̄ǹkan tí a fún ọ — imọ́lẹ̀ ni ọ jẹ́.*  
"Light is not something given to you — light is what you are."

### Putting the two together

Read in daily life, this figure asks a person to honour those who came before, settle unfinished obligations, and stop treating limits as enemies. It cautions against pride about health, wealth or status, since all of them are borrowed for a time. At the same time, when this figure is cast, tradition reads it as encouragement to act openly. Plan in the light, speak plainly, and avoid shortcuts that need to be hidden later. It also reminds a person that a good start still needs steady follow-through.

Interpretations of individual Omo Odù differ between lineages and between diviners, so treat this page as a reading aid and not a ruling. A consultation with a trained Babaláwo or Ìyánífá will always be fuller than any written summary.

content:
## Ọ̀yẹ̀kú-Ìwòrì

### Overview

Ancestral memory meets inner sight. This figure says that the answers you seek come through honest self-examination and respect for the departed.

### Governing Influences

- **Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Méjì** — endings, the ancestors, the unseen world, mortality (Ikú (Death) / Ọ̀sun)
- **Ìwòrì Méjì** — self-knowledge, hidden truth, inner vision (Ọ̀sanyìn / Ọ̀rúnmìlà)


### Guidance

Remember where you come from, and let that knowledge shape who you decide to be.

<!-- READING_START -->

### How this figure is read

In Ifá, a figure is built from two columns of four marks, read from the right column to the left. Here the right column is Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Méjì (double · double · double · double) and the left column is Ìwòrì Méjì (double · single · single · double). Many diviners start with the right column and then bring in the left, though schools of Ifá differ in how they weigh the two. Reading Ọ̀yẹ̀kú-Ìwòrì means holding both lessons together and asking how they bear on the question at hand.

### From Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Méjì

Ọ̀yẹ̀kú teaches respect for the ancestors, acceptance of mortality, and the understanding that every ending clears space for renewal. It warns against arrogance in the face of life's fragility.

*Òkú tó sun, kì í jí mọ́; ẹ̀mí tó lọ, kì í padà bí ara.*  
"The dead that sleeps does not wake again; the spirit that departs does not return in the same body."

### From Ìwòrì Méjì

Ìwòrì calls for introspection and honesty about one's own motives before judging others. It reveals secrets — both dangerous and beneficial — and teaches that true wisdom begins with self-awareness.

*Bí a kò bá mọ ara ẹni, a kì í mọ ẹlòmíràn.*  
"If one does not know oneself, one cannot truly know another."

### Putting the two together

Read in daily life, this figure asks a person to honour those who came before, settle unfinished obligations, and stop treating limits as enemies. It cautions against pride about health, wealth or status, since all of them are borrowed for a time. At the same time, tradition uses this figure to counsel reflection. Before blaming, ask what part is yours. Before trusting a story, look for what is missing from it. Insight gained this way can protect a person from deception, including self-deception.

Interpretations of individual Omo Odù differ between lineages and between diviners, so treat this page as a reading aid and not a ruling. A consultation with a trained Babaláwo or Ìyánífá will always be fuller than any written summary.

<!-- READING_END -->

title: Ọ̀yẹ̀kú-Òdí

excerpt: An ending is quietly preparing a rebirth. Like a seed in the earth, something that seems finished is transforming out of sight.
content:
## Ọ̀yẹ̀kú-Òdí

### Overview

An ending is quietly preparing a rebirth. Like a seed in the earth, something that seems finished is transforming out of sight.

### Governing Influences

- **Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Méjì** — endings, the ancestors, the unseen world, mortality (Ikú (Death) / Ọ̀sun)
- **Òdí Méjì** — the womb, mystery, transformation, hidden depth (Ọya / Yemọja)


### Guidance

Do not mourn too long. Prepare for what is growing beneath the surface.

<!-- READING_START -->

### How this figure is read

In Ifá, a figure is built from two columns of four marks, read from the right column to the left. Here the right column is Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Méjì (double · double · double · double) and the left column is Òdí Méjì (single · double · double · single). Many diviners start with the right column and then bring in the left, though schools of Ifá differ in how they weigh the two. Reading Ọ̀yẹ̀kú-Òdí means holding both lessons together and asking how they bear on the question at hand.

### From Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Méjì

Ọ̀yẹ̀kú teaches respect for the ancestors, acceptance of mortality, and the understanding that every ending clears space for renewal. It warns against arrogance in the face of life's fragility.

*Òkú tó sun, kì í jí mọ́; ẹ̀mí tó lọ, kì í padà bí ara.*  
"The dead that sleeps does not wake again; the spirit that departs does not return in the same body."

### From Òdí Méjì

Òdí teaches patience with processes that are not yet visible — pregnancy, growth, and transformation take time in darkness before they emerge into light. It also warns against forcing what must unfold naturally.

*Ohun tó wà nínú, kì í fi ara rẹ̀ hàn ní ọ̀nà kan ṣoṣo.*  
"What is within does not reveal itself in only one way."

### Putting the two together

Read in daily life, this figure asks a person to honour those who came before, settle unfinished obligations, and stop treating limits as enemies. It cautions against pride about health, wealth or status, since all of them are borrowed for a time. At the same time, in practice, this figure advises a person not to uncover a plan, a project or a relationship too early. Give it time and shelter. It also warns against forcing outcomes, because pressure applied at the wrong stage can damage what is forming.

Interpretations of individual Omo Odù differ between lineages and between diviners, so treat this page as a reading aid and not a ruling. A consultation with a trained Babaláwo or Ìyánífá will always be fuller than any written summary.

<!-- READING_END -->

## Ọ̀yẹ̀kú-Ìrosùn

### Overview

Loss and consequence are close together. There is a warning of the cost of careless actions and of the need for offerings to protect the living.

### Governing Influences

- **Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Méjì** — endings, the ancestors, the unseen world, mortality (Ikú (Death) / Ọ̀sun)
- **Ìrosùn Méjì** — blood, sacrifice, warning, consequence (Ṣàngó / Ọya)


### Guidance

Make amends where needed and perform the sacrifice that restores balance.

<!-- READING_START -->

### How this figure is read

In Ifá, a figure is built from two columns of four marks, read from the right column to the left. Here the right column is Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Méjì (double · double · double · double) and the left column is Ìrosùn Méjì (single · single · double · double). Many diviners start with the right column and then bring in the left, though schools of Ifá differ in how they weigh the two. Reading Ọ̀yẹ̀kú-Ìrosùn means holding both lessons together and asking how they bear on the question at hand.

### From Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Méjì

Ọ̀yẹ̀kú teaches respect for the ancestors, acceptance of mortality, and the understanding that every ending clears space for renewal. It warns against arrogance in the face of life's fragility.

"The dead that sleeps does not wake again; the spirit that departs does not return in the same body."

### From Ìrosùn Méjì

Ìrosùn warns that actions have irreversible consequences, and that ẹbọ (sacrifice) — whether of time, pride, or resources — is often required to avert disaster. It teaches accountability.

Change reaches the household of the ancestors. Old arrangements shift, and flexibility is the price of keeping peace in the family.

### Governing Influences

- **Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Méjì** — endings, the ancestors, the unseen world, mortality (Ikú (Death) / Ọ̀sun)
- **Ọ̀wọ́nrín Méjì** — instability, change, the trickster's lesson, humility (Èṣù / Ọ̀rúnmìlà)


### Guidance

Adapt to new circumstances in the family and hold tradition with an open hand.

<!-- READING_START -->

### How this figure is read

In Ifá, a figure is built from two columns of four marks, read from the right column to the left. Here the right column is Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Méjì (double · double · double · double) and the left column is Ọ̀wọ́nrín Méjì (double · double · single · single). *Ohun tó dúró jẹ́ẹ́, ni yíò yí padà.*  
"What stands firm today may be overturned tomorrow."

## Ọ̀yẹ̀kú-Ọ̀bàrà

### Overview

Prestige is tempered by mortality. Whatever honour you hold is temporary, and the figure urges humility and generosity with it.

### Governing Influences

- **Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Méjì** — endings, the ancestors, the unseen world, mortality (Ikú (Death) / Ọ̀sun)
- **Ọ̀bàrà Méjì** — honour, boastfulness, the danger of pride, leadership (Ṣàngó / Ọ̀bàtálá)


### Guidance

Use your position to serve others, since status will not last forever.

<!-- READING_START -->

### How this figure is read

In Ifá, a figure is built from two columns of four marks, read from the right column to the left. Here the right column is Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Méjì (double · double · double · double) and the left column is Ọ̀bàrà Méjì (single · double · double · double). Many diviners start with the right column and then bring in the left, though schools of Ifá differ in how they weigh the two. Ọ̀yẹ̀kú teaches respect for the ancestors, acceptance of mortality, and the understanding that every ending clears space for renewal. It warns against arrogance in the face of life's fragility.

"The dead that sleeps does not wake again; the spirit that departs does not return in the same body."

### From Ọ̀bàrà Méjì

Ọ̀bàrà teaches that leadership and confidence are gifts, but boastfulness invites downfall. True honour is shown through humility and generosity, not empty declarations.

*Ìgbéraga ni í tẹ̀lé àṣejù ìṣọ́ra.*  
"Excess confidence is often followed by a fall."

### Putting the two together

Read in daily life, this figure asks a person to honour those who came before, settle unfinished obligations, and stop treating limits as enemies. It cautions against pride about health, wealth or status, since all of them are borrowed for a time. At the same time, read practically, this figure advises that a person should let results speak. Say less than you can do, deliver what you say, and share credit. Reputation built that way is stronger than one built on announcements.

Interpretations of individual Omo Odù differ between lineages and between diviners, so treat this page as a reading aid and not a ruling. A consultation with a trained Babaláwo or Ìyánífá will always be fuller than any written summary.

<!-- READING_END -->

## Ọ̀yẹ̀kú-Ọ̀kànràn

### Overview

Hard truths surface around loss or inheritance. Conflict may rise, and honesty with the family is what lets it settle.

### Governing Influences

- **Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Méjì** — endings, the ancestors, the unseen world, mortality (Ikú (Death) / Ọ̀sun)
- **Ọ̀kànràn Méjì** — conflict, truth-telling, sharp consequences (Ọya / Ògún)


### Guidance

Resolve disputes openly and fairly, especially over what the departed have left behind.

<!-- READING_START -->

### How this figure is read

In Ifá, a figure is built from two columns of four marks, read from the right column to the left. Here the right column is Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Méjì (double · double · double · double) and the left column is Ọ̀kànràn Méjì (double · double · double · single). Many diviners start with the right column and then bring in the left, though schools of Ifá differ in how they weigh the two. Reading Ọ̀yẹ̀kú-Ọ̀kànràn means holding both lessons together and asking how they bear on the question at hand.

### From Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Méjì

Ọ̀yẹ̀kú teaches respect for the ancestors, acceptance of mortality, and the understanding that every ending clears space for renewal. It warns against arrogance in the face of life's fragility.

*Òkú tó sun, kì í jí mọ́; ẹ̀mí tó lọ, kì í padà bí ara.*  
"The dead that sleeps does not wake again; the spirit that departs does not return in the same body."

### From Ọ̀kànràn Méjì

Ọ̀kànràn exposes what is hidden and warns against betrayal, gossip, and dishonesty. It teaches that confronting conflict honestly, though painful, prevents greater harm later.

*Òtítọ́ máa ń dùn, ṣùgbọ́n irọ́ máa ń pa ni níkẹyìn.*  
"Truth may sting, but a lie eventually destroys."

### Putting the two together

Read in daily life, this figure asks a person to honour those who came before, settle unfinished obligations, and stop treating limits as enemies. It cautions against pride about health, wealth or status, since all of them are borrowed for a time. At the same time, in everyday terms, this figure advises resolving disputes directly rather than letting them grow in silence. It also asks a person to think before speaking, because words once said cannot be taken back.

Interpretations of individual Omo Odù differ between lineages and between diviners, so treat this page as a reading aid and not a ruling. A consultation with a trained Babaláwo or Ìyánífá will always be fuller than any written summary.

<!-- READING_END -->

## Ọ̀yẹ̀kú-Ògúndá

### Overview

The path is cleared through effort and respect for the dead. Work and ritual are two parts of the same duty.

### Governing Influences

- **Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Méjì** — endings, the ancestors, the unseen world, mortality (Ikú (Death) / Ọ̀sun)
- **Ògúndá Méjì** — struggle, tools, perseverance, clearing the path (Ògún)


### Guidance

Persevere in your labour and do not neglect your spiritual obligations.

<!-- READING_START -->

### How this figure is read

In Ifá, a figure is built from two columns of four marks, read from the right column to the left. Here the right column is Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Méjì (double · double · double · double) and the left column is Ògúndá Méjì (single · single · single · double). Many diviners start with the right column and then bring in the left, though schools of Ifá differ in how they weigh the two. Reading Ọ̀yẹ̀kú-Ògúndá means holding both lessons together and asking how they bear on the question at hand.

### From Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Méjì

Ọ̀yẹ̀kú teaches respect for the ancestors, acceptance of mortality, and the understanding that every ending clears space for renewal. It warns against arrogance in the face of life's fragility.

*Òkú tó sun, kì í jí mọ́; ẹ̀mí tó lọ, kì í padà bí ara.*  
"The dead that sleeps does not wake again; the spirit that departs does not return in the same body."

### From Ògúndá Méjì

Ògúndá honours the warrior spirit of Ògún — perseverance, the courage to clear obstacles, and the discipline of using one's tools and skills wisely rather than recklessly.

*Ọ̀nà tí a kò gbóná, a kì í rìn án láìsí ọgbọ́n.*  
"A path that has not been cleared cannot be walked without skill and effort."

### Putting the two together

Read in daily life, this figure asks a person to honour those who came before, settle unfinished obligations, and stop treating limits as enemies. It cautions against pride about health, wealth or status, since all of them are borrowed for a time. At the same time, this figure reads as encouragement to keep working at a difficult task and to prepare the right tools before starting. It also cautions that power without restraint becomes destructive, so strength should be directed by purpose.

Interpretations of individual Omo Odù differ between lineages and between diviners, so treat this page as a reading aid and not a ruling. A consultation with a trained Babaláwo or Ìyánífá will always be fuller than any written summary.

<!-- READING_END -->

## Ọ̀yẹ̀kú-Ọ̀sá

### Overview

Turbulence stirs the realm of the ancestors. There is a warning of sudden upheaval and advises calm, protective action.

### Governing Influences

- **Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Méjì** — endings, the ancestors, the unseen world, mortality (Ikú (Death) / Ọ̀sun)
- **Ọ̀sá Méjì** — upheaval, the whirlwind, sudden change, protection from harm (Ọya)


### Guidance

Stay composed in a crisis and seek spiritual cover before making big decisions.

<!-- READING_START -->

### How this figure is read

In Ifá, a figure is built from two columns of four marks, read from the right column to the left. Here the right column is Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Méjì (double · double · double · double) and the left column is Ọ̀sá Méjì (double · single · single · single). Many diviners start with the right column and then bring in the left, though schools of Ifá differ in how they weigh the two. Reading Ọ̀yẹ̀kú-Ọ̀sá means holding both lessons together and asking how they bear on the question at hand.

### From Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Méjì

Ọ̀yẹ̀kú teaches respect for the ancestors, acceptance of mortality, and the understanding that every ending clears space for renewal. It warns against arrogance in the face of life's fragility.

*Òkú tó sun, kì í jí mọ́; ẹ̀mí tó lọ, kì í padà bí ara.*  
"The dead that sleeps does not wake again; the spirit that departs does not return in the same body."

### From Ọ̀sá Méjì

Ọ̀sá teaches resilience through sudden disruption. What feels destructive can also clear away what no longer serves growth. It calls for protection (ẹbọ) and steady faith during turbulent seasons.

*Afẹ́fẹ́ tó le kì í fi ìgi sílẹ̀ láìṣí àyípadà.*  
"A strong wind never leaves a tree unchanged."

### Putting the two together

Read in daily life, this figure asks a person to honour those who came before, settle unfinished obligations, and stop treating limits as enemies. It cautions against pride about health, wealth or status, since all of them are borrowed for a time. At the same time, practically, this figure advises preparation and calm. Keep essentials secure, avoid reacting to every disturbance, and look for what the change makes possible once it settles.

Interpretations of individual Omo Odù differ between lineages and between diviners, so treat this page as a reading aid and not a ruling. A consultation with a trained Babaláwo or Ìyánífá will always be fuller than any written summary.

<!-- READING_END -->

## Ọ̀yẹ̀kú-Ìká

### Overview

Resentment threatens to harm the living. It advises restraint and reconciliation so that bitterness does not grow into loss.

### Governing Influences

- **Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Méjì** — endings, the ancestors, the unseen world, mortality (Ikú (Death) / Ọ̀sun)
- **Ìká Méjì** — cruelty, resentment, the need for restraint (Ọya / Èṣù)


### Guidance

Let go of grudges and mend broken relationships while there is time.

<!-- READING_START -->

### How this figure is read

In Ifá, a figure is built from two columns of four marks, read from the right column to the left. Here the right column is Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Méjì (double · double · double · double) and the left column is Ìká Méjì (double · single · double · double). Many diviners start with the right column and then bring in the left, though schools of Ifá differ in how they weigh the two. Reading Ọ̀yẹ̀kú-Ìká means holding both lessons together and asking how they bear on the question at hand.

### From Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Méjì

Ọ̀yẹ̀kú teaches respect for the ancestors, acceptance of mortality, and the understanding that every ending clears space for renewal. It warns against arrogance in the face of life's fragility.

*Òkú tó sun, kì í jí mọ́; ẹ̀mí tó lọ, kì í padà bí ara.*  
"The dead that sleeps does not wake again; the spirit that departs does not return in the same body."

### From Ìká Méjì

Ìká warns of the dangers of bitterness, envy, and vengeance — both suffering it and inflicting it. It teaches restraint, forgiveness, and guarding one's heart against becoming hardened by pain.

*Ìkà ọkàn kì í mú àlàáfíà wá.*  
"A cruel heart never brings peace."

### Putting the two together

Read in daily life, this figure asks a person to honour those who came before, settle unfinished obligations, and stop treating limits as enemies. It cautions against pride about health, wealth or status, since all of them are borrowed for a time. At the same time, this figure counsels watchfulness over one's own heart. If someone has wronged you, address it but do not let it define you. It also advises caution around people whose behaviour is driven by resentment.

Interpretations of individual Omo Odù differ between lineages and between diviners, so treat this page as a reading aid and not a ruling. A consultation with a trained Babaláwo or Ìyánífá will always be fuller than any written summary.

<!-- READING_END -->

## Ọ̀yẹ̀kú-Òtúrúpọ̀n

### Overview

Sickness and the thin boundary of life appear together. It advises prompt care, patience and attention to the elderly and ill.

### Governing Influences

- **Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Méjì** — endings, the ancestors, the unseen world, mortality (Ikú (Death) / Ọ̀sun)
- **Òtúrúpọ̀n Méjì** — illness and healing, secrets of the body, patience (Ọbàtálá / Ọ̀rúnmìlà)


### Guidance

Look after the sick, seek treatment early, and do not delay the healing.

<!-- READING_START -->

### How this figure is read

In Ifá, a figure is built from two columns of four marks, read from the right column to the left. Here the right column is Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Méjì (double · double · double · double) and the left column is Òtúrúpọ̀n Méjì (double · double · single · double). Many diviners start with the right column and then bring in the left, though schools of Ifá differ in how they weigh the two. Reading Ọ̀yẹ̀kú-Òtúrúpọ̀n means holding both lessons together and asking how they bear on the question at hand.

### From Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Méjì

Ọ̀yẹ̀kú teaches respect for the ancestors, acceptance of mortality, and the understanding that every ending clears space for renewal. It warns against arrogance in the face of life's fragility.

*Òkú tó sun, kì í jí mọ́; ẹ̀mí tó lọ, kì í padà bí ara.*  
"The dead that sleeps does not wake again; the spirit that departs does not return in the same body."

### From Òtúrúpọ̀n Méjì

Òtúrúpọ̀n calls for patience, proper diagnosis before action, and respect for the body's natural healing processes. It also symbolises the wisdom that comes from surviving hardship.

*Àrùn tí a kò tọ́jú lọ́nà tí ó tọ́ kì í yá.*  
"An illness not treated in the right way does not heal."

### Putting the two together

Read in daily life, this figure asks a person to honour those who came before, settle unfinished obligations, and stop treating limits as enemies. It cautions against pride about health, wealth or status, since all of them are borrowed for a time. At the same time, read in daily life, this figure advises seeking the right help early, following treatment through, and resting enough. It also encourages care for people who are unwell, since recovery is helped by support.

Interpretations of individual Omo Odù differ between lineages and between diviners, so treat this page as a reading aid and not a ruling. A consultation with a trained Babaláwo or Ìyánífá will always be fuller than any written summary.

<!-- READING_END -->
